background.definition: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant collagen vascular disease caused by mutations in FBN1, the gene that encodes fibrillin 1. Patients with Marfan syndrome most notably have abnormalities of the skeletal, cardiovascular, and ocular systems, but may also have skin, pulmonary, and muscle involvement.

list.listitem: One study estimates that Marfan syndrome occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 live births.
Due to the difficulty in recognizing Marfan syndrome, varying manifestations with age, and the lack of a gold standard for diagnosis, this number likely underestimates the true incidence.
In a recent study using a national database in Taiwan, the overall prevalence was 10.2 (95% CI, 9.8-10.7) per 100,000 individuals.

In one case series of 20 children with Marfan syndrome, the children had significantly lower bone mineral density in whole body and lumbar spine after adjusting results for height, age, gender, and ethnicity.

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is about 6-times more common among individuals with Marfan syndrome vs. the general population based on six studies, with a prevalence rate estimate of 59.7% (95% CI, 39.7-77.0). Treatment of OSA with continuous positive airway pressure appears to decrease fluctuations in systolic blood pressure and lowers morning D-dimer levels.

Authors of a systematic review of cross-sectional studies found that patients with Marfan syndrome report decreased quality of life; challenges in education, work and family life; and increased risk of depression and anxiety.
The main cause of Marfan syndrome is a mutation in the FBN1 gene in chromosome band 15q21.1.
It follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.
The majority are family specific point mutations but approximately 25% arise from a new mutation.
Fibrillin 1 is a key component of extracellular matrix elastic fibers and a negative regulator of cytokine transforming growth factor B.
Deficiency in fibrillin 1 leads to excessive activation of transforming growth factor B, which results in matrix metalloproteinase activation and extracellular matrix degeneration.
Changes in the walls of elastic arteries occur in the media, and progress over time as person ages.

Fibrillin 1 mutations can be classified as dominant negative (incorporation of non-mutated and mutated fibrillin-1 in the extracellular matrix) or having haploinsufficiency (only incorporation of non-mutated fibrillin-1 resulting in a decreased amount of fibrillin-1 protein). Investigators found an association between the haploinsufficiency mutation, present in 113/290 (39%) of patients, and a more severely affected aortic phenotype with larger aortic root diameters and a more rapid dilation rate with a trend towards increased aortic dissection and death.
Offer genetic counseling to affected individuals. C
Preparticipation sports physicals should include assessment for physical stigmata of Marfan syndrome, which should prompt further evaluation prior to clearance.C
Although β-blockers are widely recommended, they have not been shown in clinical trials to prevent cardiovascular complications.
Treatment with ACE inhibitors or ARBs also reduce rates of aortic dilation but also have no demonstrated effect on cardiovascular outcomes.
Trial data are presented under drug treatment.

list.listitem: Suspect Marfan syndrome in patients with a tall, thin body; long limbs; arachnodactyly; pectus deformities (excavatum and carinatum); and scoliosis. Patients may have cardiac findings, including aortic valve incompetence and mitral valve prolapse. Typical ophthalmologic findings include myopia and lens dislocation (ectopia lentis).

The American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) recommend diagnosing Marfan syndrome in patients with no family history if they have any one of the following: a dilated aortic root (defined as greater than or equal to two standard deviations above the mean for age, sex, and body surface area) and ectopia lentis; a dilated aortic root and a mutation in FBN1 that is clearly pathologic; a dilated aortic root and multiple systemic features, or ectopia lentis and a mutation in FBN1 that has previously been associated with aortic disease.

For patients with a family history, diagnose Marfan syndrome if they have any one of the following: ectopia lentis, multiple systemic features (see below) or a dilated aortic root (if over age 20 years, greater than two standard deviations; if younger than 20 years, greater than three standard deviations).

Clinical indicators of arachnodactyly can be elicited by the wrist test and the thumb test. In the wrist test, the patient grasps the opposite wrist between the thumb and fifth ("pinky") finger. An abnormal test result is when the thumb overlaps the terminal phalanx of the pinky. In the thumb test, the patient clenches their hand over the thumb. The result is abnormal if the entire nail of the thumb projects beyond the ulnar border of the hand.
Cutaneous striae, especially in areas other than the buttock, hip, or thigh, increase the likelihood of Marfan syndrome.

A study reported the following percentages of patients ultimately diagnosed based on their initial reason for referral: skeletal abnormalities (36%), ocular symptoms (78%), cardiovascular abnormalities (41%), and family history (31%).
Among patients with pectus excavatum and a dilated aortic root, approximately 40% have Marfan syndrome.

Lesser known symptoms and disorders reported by clinical experts conducting literature reviews include arrythmias; restrictive and parenchymal lung disease; OSA; liver and kidney cysts; biliary tract disease; diaphragmatic hernia; adiposity; urinary incontinence; myopathy; reduced bone mineral density; craniofacial manifestations and craniomandibular dysfunction; atrophic scars; headache from migraine and spontaneous cerebrospinal fluid leakage; cognitive dysfunction; schizophrenia; depression; fatigue; pain; activated fibrinolysis, thrombin, platelets, and acquired von Willebrand disease, and platelet dysfunction.
Pain at several anatomic sites appears to be common in patients with Marfan syndrome with prevalence rates varying from 47% to 92%.

Refer patients with suspected Marfan syndrome for echocardiography to assess the aortic root, and for a slit lamp examination to assess their lenses. Patients with Marfan syndrome also have larger left ventricular volume and poorer left ventricular function with lower left ventricular ejection fraction than matched controls.
Among patients with pectus excavatum and a dilated aortic root on echocardiography, approximately 40% have Marfan syndrome.
Up to two thirds of patients with Marfan syndrome have radiographically proven scoliosis and the presence of biconcave vertebrae ("codfish" vertebrae).
Consider CT or MRI in patients with evidence of lumbosacral dural ectasia and protrusion acetabulae.

Mutations of FBN1 are present in approximately two thirds of patients fulfilling the diagnostic criteria for Marfan syndrome. However, since as many as 46 specific genetic mutations exist, the role of genetic testing is unclear.

In a German study, a clinical prediction rule using seven variables (ectopia lentis [4 points]; family history of Marfan syndrome [2 points]; and previous thoracic aortic surgery, pectus excavatum, wrist and thumb sign, previous pneumothorax, or skin striae [1 point each]) was useful for screening for Marfan syndrome. Patients with a total score of >3.5 points had a high probability of Marfan syndrome (92% derivation set and 91% validation set).
Suspect Marfan syndrome in patients with a tall, thin body; long limbs; arachnodactyly; pectus deformities; and scoliosis.
Apply the diagnostic criteria in and .
Obtain an echocardiogram and dilated eye exam.
To confirm the diagnosis, refer the patient to a genetics clinic for molecular and genetic testing.
Although β-blockers are widely recommended and reduce rates of aortic dilation, they have not been shown in clinical trials to be effective in preventing cardiovascular complications.A
Treatment with ACE inhibitors B or ARBs reduce rates of aortic dilation to a similar degree but also have no demonstrated effect on cardiovascular outcomes.A
According to a decision analysis, outcomes are better when prophylactic repair of the aorta is performed when the aortic root diameter is between 3.0 and 3.5 cm.B

Treatment is aimed at preventing or slowing the rate of aortic root dilatation, as the major life-threatening complications are aortic regurgitation, dissection, and rupture, which are directly related to the size of the aortic root.

Although it is widely recommended that patients with Marfan syndrome receive β-blockers to prevent cardiovascular complications, a meta-analysis of six small clinical trials with 802 patients found that the 22% of patients who took β-blockers had bad cardiovascular outcomes (death or major morbidity) compared with 20% of control patients.

In a more recent attempted meta-analysis, authors were only able to identify a single, open-label RCT with 70 participants with Marfan syndrome that met inclusion criteria; this trial showed no differences at about 9 years between propranolol and no treatment on all-cause mortality, aortic dissection, aortic regurgitation, cardiovascular surgery or congestive heart failure despite a reduced rate of aortic dilatation measured by M-mode echocardiography in the treatment group.

Based on an individual patient data meta-analysis of 3 trials including 766 participants that compared ARBs with β blockers, at a follow-up of 3 years the annual change in the aortic root Z score was similar in the two group and superior to untreated controls.

listitem.strong: Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs)

list.listitem: ACE inhibitors reduce aortic stiffness, improve distensibility, and slow the rate of aortic dilation. In one study, compared with beta-blockers, 2 of 32 patients taking ACE inhibitors died or had aortic root replacement compared with 8 of 25 patients taking β-blockers.

Authors of a systematic review of 6 RCTs found losartan significantly decreased the rate of aortic dilatation compared with non-losartan treatment, however, there was no benefit on clinical outcomes including cardiovascular surgery or death.

Based on an individual patient data meta-analysis of 3 trials including 766 participants that compared ARBs with β blockers, at a follow-up of 3 years the annual change in the aortic root Z score was similar in the two group and superior to untreated controls.

In a multicenter RCT of 608 children and young adults with Marfan syndrome, there was no significant difference in the rate of aortic-root dilatation over 3 years for those randomized to atenolol or losartan, an ARB. There were no significant differences at 3 years in adverse event rates (40 vs. 50, respectively), dissection events (0 vs. 2), or aortic root surgery (10 vs. 18, respectively). The 3-year rate of aortic-root surgery was higher among young adults vs. children (8.5% vs. 3.8%).

Similarly, there were no differences in aortic-root progression were seen in another RCT comparing use of losartan with atenolol or in an open label follow-up of a previous RCT. In the latter study, after follow-up of 6.7 ± 1.5 years, nine events (14.1%) occurred in the losartan group and 12 (18.8%) in the atenolol group with survival analysis showing no differences in the combined endpoint of aortic surgery, aortic dissection, or death.

A study randomized 233 adults with Marfan syndrome to addition of losartan to usual care (71% were taking beta-blockers) or usual care alone. After the 3 year trial, 75 patients continued losartan and 78 in the usual care group did not add it. After a median 8 years, patients using losartan had fewer deaths (0 vs. 5, p = 0.014), fewer aortic dissections (3 vs. 11, p = 0.013), and no difference in elective aortic root replacements (10 vs. 13, p = 0.264).
Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 trials found that monotherapy with either β-blockers or ARBs did not differ significantly in changes in aortic growth or cardiovascular events.

In a 5-year RCT of 192 subjects with Marfan syndrome and a mean age of 18 years, use of irbesartan, a long-acting selective ARB, after a run-in period, reduced aortic root dilation with a mean difference of -0.22 mm annually vs. placebo. However, there were no differences in other outcomes including aortic surgical procedures, which occurred in 5 vs. 4 patients on placebo, or serious adverse events (~25% in both groups). Half of the subjects were also taking β-blockers.

Beginning in Summer 2018, the Federal Drug Administration learned and reported that some generic versions of ARB medications contained nitrosamine impurities that don’t meet the agency’s safety standards. This led to a recall of certain lot numbers in both the US and Canada. Information can be found at https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/recalls-angiotensin-ii-receptor-blockers-arbs-including-valsartan-losartan-and-irbesartan (accessed May 2021).
Combination losartan and β-blockers did not reduce aortic growth or improve cardiac function over β-blockers alone at 3 years in a small RCT of 22 patients with Marfan syndrome.

However, in long-term (up to 8 years) follow-up of 153 of the original 233 people with Marfan syndrome enrolled in the COMPARE trial, the 75 patients randomized to losartan® plus usual treatment, which included β-blockers in 71%, who continued losartan had significantly fewer deaths (0 vs. 5) and aortic dissection (3 vs. 11) than the 78 patients originally allocated to the control group who never used losartan after inclusion.

Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 9 trials involving 1,449 patients concluded that aortic root dilation was significantly less with combination ARB plus beta-blocker than beta-blockers alone, although there were no significant differences in other aortic dilation-related measures and no reported patient-oriented outcome measures.
According to a decision analysis, outcomes are better when prophylactic repair of the aorta is performed when the aortic root diameter is between 3.0 and 3.5 cm.
ACMG recommends surgical repair for aortic measurements >4.5 cm, a rate of increase in size >1 cm/year, or progressive aortic regurgitation.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 cohort studies reporting on outcomes of 2,976 patients with Marfan syndrome undergoing aortic root surgery found valve-sparing root replacement, performed in 1,352 patients, was associated with a reduced risk of thromboembolism (OR 0.32; 95% CI, 0.16-0.62), late hemorrhagic complications (OR 0.18; 95% CI, 0.07-0.45) endocarditis (OR 0.27; 95% CI, 0.10-0.68) and reintervention rates (OR 0.89; 95% CI, 0.35-2.24) compared to the 1,624 patients treated with composite valve graft (CVG) surgery.

In a study of 316 patients with Marfan syndrome, aortic valve-sparing and aortic valve-replacing aortic root replacement results were similar for major complications and one-year survival, but more patients with valve-sparing surgery had aortic regurgitation of at least moderate severity at one year (7% vs. 0% in the valve-replacing group).

Reimplantation of the aortic valve was found to be superior to CVG for in-hospital mortality rate (OR 0.23; 95% CI, 0.09-0.55) and long-term survival (93.1% [95% CI, 66.4-100] vs. 82.6% [95% CI, 74.9-89.2]) based on a review of 20 retrospective studies with 2156 patients.

In a meta-analysis of stent grafting in patients with Marfan syndrome and type B dissection, authors found low operative risk (1.9%) but substantial risk of complications (primarily endoleaks and surgical conversions) and death at midterm follow-up. The authors caution against routine use of endovascular stent grafting.

In a case series of 61 patients with Marfan syndrome and mitral regurgitation, patients had better 10-year survival with valve repair than valve replacement (80% [N = 40] vs. 41% [N = 21], respectively); there was no difference in re-intervention rate. Concomitant aortic repair occurred in similar percentages (45% vs. 43%, respectively). Survival with repair was similar to survival for patients with myxomatous mitral disease repair.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 studies including 120 patients with Marfan syndrome and Stanford type B aortic dissection found thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) was associated with low perioperative morbidity (e.g., 15.2% endoleaks) and in-hospital mortality (3.7%), but was associated with a high rate of late reintervention (repeat TEVAR was performed in 15.5% and open aortic surgery in 18.6%).
Marfan syndrome is a risk factor for spontaneous coronary artery dissection as a cause of acute myocardial infarction (OR 4.7, 95% CI 1.7 to 12.5).

A study performed MRA in a consecutive series of Marfan syndrome patients, and found 3 with undiagnosed intracranial aneurysm. This is lower than previous series (8.9%) but the authors speculate that previous studies may have been subject to selection bias.

An approach to patients with suspected acute aortic syndromes can be found in the 2022 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease. Patients often present with abrupt onset of severe “sharp” or “stabbing” pain in the chest or back in addition to other symptoms. Acute aortic dissection risk scoring systems (eg, aortic dissection detection risk score [AAD-RS] or aorta simplified score [AORTAs]) can aid in the evaluation. For the latter score, the presence of shock or more than one of the following places patients at high probability of aortic dissection: aneurysm, pulse deficit, neurologic deficit, severe pain, or sudden onset pain. CT is recommended as initial diagnostic imaging; transesophageal echocardiography and magnetic resonance imaging are reasonable alternatives. Finally, the recommended initial management by the guidelines includes care in an ICU setting with anti-impulse therapy with invasive monitoring and intravenous beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, and pain management.

Aortic dissection is misdiagnosed in about 33% of patients. In this meta-analysis, factors associated with misdiagnosis included presence of symptoms and features associated with other diseases (e.g., acute coronary syndrome, stroke and pulmonary embolism), absence of typical features (e.g., widened mediastinum on chest X-ray) or concurrent congestive heart failure. Factors associated with more accurate diagnosis included comprehensive history taking and increased use of imaging.

In an uncontrolled study of 24 patients with Marfan syndrome and scoliosis up to 45 degrees, only 17% of patients treated with a brace stabilized (did not progress beyond 45 degrees or slowed to less than 5 degrees) after 24 months; sixteen of the 24 patients were advised to have surgical correction.

In a small cohort study, use of a high-density pedicle screw construct contributed to improved correction of thoracic curves in patients with Marfan syndrome and thoracic curves ≥70°, but all patients improved post-operatively on the SRS-22 questionnaire with no differences between groups.
Surgical correction of lenticular and musculoskeletal complications of Marfan syndrome are often performed, although randomized trials do not exist.

In one Chinese RCT of 49 patients and 71 eyes with subluxed lens, there was no significant difference in best corrected vision between phaco-emulsification combined with scleral-fixated posterior chamber intraocular lens or iris-fixated anterior chamber intraocular lens implantation, although, at 1 year, decentration of the intraocular lens was found in 19 eyes (48.7%) in the scleral-fixated posterior chamber intraocular lens group vs. none in the iris-fixated anterior chamber intraocular lens group.

Although guidelines recommend against heavy exercise in patients with thoracic aortic disease and blood pressure elevation during exercise may be associated with an increased risk of acute aortic dissection, there are no longitudinal controlled trials that have evaluated the effect of exercise on survival or risk of aortic dissection in patients with Marfan syndrome with thoracic aortic disease.

Use of a 6-week intervention with a self-help book and telephone-based peer counseling for patients with rare chronic diseases including Marfan syndrome resulted in higher rates of acceptance of the disease (primary outcome) and improvement in several secondary outcomes (i.e., coping strategies, social support, and mental quality of life) compared with usual care.
Obtain ophthalmologic examination yearly to evaluate for ectopia lentis, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and cataracts.
Patients should have a cardiac evaluation at least yearly after the discovery of aortic enlargement.
Patients should have orthopedic evaluation for progressive scoliosis and pectus deformities (excavatum and carinatum).

In the era before the use of surgery for proximal aortic aneurysms, affected patients died approximately 20 years before unaffected patients, and up to 90% of their deaths were due to aortic dissection.B
In 1973, the average life expectancy of a patient with Marfan syndrome was 48 years; in 1980, it had increased to 72 years.B
Cardiac manifestations (mitral valve and aortic root abnormalities) often begin silently at a young age, but usually become clinically significant by the second decade.B

Independent risk factors for dissection of the descending aorta (Type B), which occurred in 54 of 600 patients in one study, were prior prophylactic aortic surgery and a proximal descending aorta diameter ≥27 mm. In the risk model, the 10-year occurrence of type B aortic dissection was 6% in low-risk patients and 34% in high-risk patients.
In another study, aortic tortuosity was a predictor of aortic dissection and/or aortic surgery and aortic dilatation rate.

In a Japanese case series of 20 consecutive patients with Marfan syndrome who underwent dissecting thoracoabdominal aorta repair (median age, 45 years; range, 19-65 years), survival at 8 years was 90 ± 9.0%. Two patients required additional aortic procedures (total arch replacement and aortic valve-sparing surgery).

If the aortic root is less than 4 cm, most patients are only minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic. If the aortic root is 4 cm or larger, or if there is moderate aortic insufficiency, there is an increased risk of progression. Authors of a systematic review of 12 papers concluded that women with Marfan syndrome are at high risk of aortic dissection during pregnancy and tthose with aortic root 4.1 to 4.5 cm should consider avoiding pregnancy.

In a review and meta-analysis of 11 reports including 85 pregnant women who suffered acute aortic dissection, of whom 44 had Marfan syndrome, 46 (61%) had dissection during pregnancy and 30 (39%) during puerperium. Surgery was performed in 73%, and maternal and fetal mortality was 23% and 27%, respectively.
Recommend baseline echocardiogram, close surveillance with routine echocardiograms, and delivery by the least hemodynamically stressful means.
Chorionic villus sampling can detect fibrillin-1 mutations in the fetus of pregnant women with Marfan syndrome.

In a small case series of 29 pregnancies in 21 women with Marfan syndrome, cardiac complications occurred in five pregnancies with one woman experiencing an ascending aortic dissection; two women required cardiac surgery within 6 months of delivery. Compared to healthy controls, women with Marfan syndrome had a higher risk of postpartum hemorrhage (OR 8.46; 95% CI, 2.52-28.38) and small for gestational age infants (24% vs. 6% in controls; OR 4.95, 95% CI, 1.58-15.55).
One group of authors identified preterm labor as a complication of Marfan syndrome.

Manifestations of Marfan syndrome have been reported in fetuses and newborns. In one literature review of 55 cases, the most frequent prenatal findings were cardiomegaly, dilatation of the great vessels and mitral or tricuspid regurgitation; for postnatally-diagnosed cases, the most frequent findings were arachnodactyly, dilatation of the great vessels and mitral or tricuspid regurgitation. Mortality rate during the first 15 months after birth was 73.68% in the prenatal group and 61.11% in the postnatal group.
Preparticipation sports physicals should include assessment for physical stigmata of Marfan syndrome, which should prompt further evaluation prior to clearance.

Among 52 children with Marfan syndrome, 46 had mitral valve prolapse, 80% of these patients were asymptomatic. After approximately 8 years of follow-up, 21 of the 46 patients had progression, 6 of whom required valve surgery.
Among these same children, aortic dilatation occurred in 43 and aortic regurgitation occurred in 13. Aortic surgery was performed in 10 of the children; 2 died.
In a small cohort study of children followed-up for up to 4 years, those who were using ARBs had a slower rate of aortic root dilation than control patients.
Bone and muscle mass are decreased in children with Marfan syndrome compared to healthy age-matched controls.
Children with Marfan syndrome also report reduced quality of life on physical and psychosocial domains compared to healthy children population norms.

cell.label: Meets any of the following: ectopia lentis; multiple systemic features (see ); or a dilated aortic root (if over 20 years, greater than two standard deviations; if younger than 20, greater than three standard deviations)?
Does not meet diagnostic standard, consider alternate diagnosis
Meets diagnostic standard; refer to geneticist for confirmation

Meets any of the following: a dilated aortic root (≥two standard deviations above the mean for age, sex, and body surface area) and ectopia lentis; a dilated aortic root and a mutation in FBN1 that is clearly pathologic; a dilated aortic root and multiple systemic features (see ); or ectopia lentis and a mutation in FBN1 that has previously been associated with aortic disease?
Does not meet diagnostic standard, consider alternate diagnosis

feature.caption: Criteria for Systemic Involvement (Multiple Systemic Features of Marfan Syndrome).

tr.td: Reduced upper‐to‐lower segment ratio AND increased arm/height AND no severe scoliosis
Facial features (three of five including dolichocephaly, enophthalmos, downslanting palpebral fissures, malar hypoplasia, and retrognathia)
*Maximum total: 20 points; score of 7 or more indicates systemic involvement

Information from: Pyeritz RE; American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics. Evaluation of the adolescent or adult with some features of Marfan syndrome. Genet Med 2012;14:171‐177. (PMID: 22237449)
